Its contents list Parts I–IV: business, risks, properties and legal matters; market and stockholder information, management analysis, financial statements, controls and disclosures; governance, compensation, ownership and related-party matters; and exhibits, schedules, and a 10-K summary.

Statements of belief may rely on incomplete information and are inherently uncertain.

title: PART I

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS Our Company
ITEM 1. BUSINESS Our Company (intro)
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its evolution from PC graphics into accelerated computing for gaming, AI, data science, scientific computing, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and metaverse applications. It explains GPU-powered deep learning and emerging uses such as recommendation systems, large language models, and generative AI; its unified hardware-and-software platform strategy, developer ecosystem, and innovation history, including GPUs and CUDA; and applications across gaming, research, cloud services, enterprise, transportation, healthcare, finance, and design. The text gives company background, notes the 2022 termination of its planned Arm acquisition and $1.35 billion write-off, defines its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments, and introduces its four markets—Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive—with an overview of the Data Center platform and AI/HPC acceleration.

nodes.title: NVIDIA’s Businesses, Markets, and Arm Deal Termination
key_items: Termination of the Arm Share Purchase Agreement
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s GPUs and accelerated computing platforms serve cloud and consumer internet providers, enterprises and startups across industries, and professional designers. Founded in 1993 and headquartered in Santa Clara, NVIDIA terminated its planned Arm acquisition from SoftBank in February 2022 due to regulatory challenges, recording a $1.35 billion write-off in fiscal 2023. Its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments span data center, networking, automotive, robotics, AI software, gaming, visualization, and metaverse products. NVIDIA focuses on four markets: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.

nodes.title: Data Center
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s data-center platform combines energy-efficient GPUs, DPUs, interconnects, systems, CUDA, and extensive software to accelerate AI, analytics, graphics, and scientific computing across cloud, enterprise, public-sector, and edge environments, improving performance and power efficiency over CPU-only systems. The text explains deep learning, machine learning, and HPC; describes industry partnerships and AI uses; and outlines GPU systems and reference designs, Hopper/H100 capabilities, planned AI cloud services, and InfiniBand/Ethernet networking. It covers BlueField DPUs and DOCA, planned Grace CPUs, full-stack software and NGC, plus paid AI Enterprise and vGPU offerings.

nodes.title: Gaming and Professional Visualization
nodes.summary: Gaming is a major entertainment market driven by premium games, esports, social connectivity, streamers, modders, and creators. NVIDIA GPUs and software enhance gaming through RTX ray tracing and DLSS; products include GeForce GPUs, GeForce NOW, SHIELD, and console chips and services. The fiscal 2023 GeForce RTX 40 Series, based on Ada Lovelace, added newer RTX, DLSS, and Tensor Core generations for up to four times previous-generation performance. In professional visualization, NVIDIA works with software vendors to advance design, manufacturing, and content-creation workflows. RTX enables real-time photorealistic rendering and is supported by leading applications. Omniverse supports 3D collaboration and virtual-world workflows; Omniverse, VR, and AR are used in enterprise applications including showrooms, training, architecture, and historical experiences.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s automotive business spans autonomous vehicles, AI cockpits, electric-vehicle computing, and infotainment. Its DRIVE Hyperion end-to-end platform supports autonomous driving and driver assistance, combining GPU-based AI training with in-vehicle perception, fusion, planning, and control. Developed with hundreds of automotive partners, it includes DRIVE AGX hardware, sensors, and modular software for driving, mapping, parking, intelligent cabin experiences, and conversational AI. DRIVE Sim provides data-center simulation for cockpit development and self-driving testing and validation. NVIDIA’s software-defined approach enables ongoing development and over-the-air feature updates.

nodes.title: Business Strategies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s strategy centers on a unified accelerated-computing platform shared across data center, gaming, visualization, and automotive; extending leadership in AI and graphics through integrated hardware, software, developer ecosystems, training, and cloud services; advancing its DRIVE autonomous-vehicle platform with partners; and licensing or custom-developing its IP. Sales and marketing rely on global teams, technical support, industry partners, developer engagement, and direct channels. Revenue can be seasonal, though fiscal 2023 patterns differed. Manufacturing is fabless, outsourcing production stages to qualified suppliers while NVIDIA may procure selected materials.

nodes.title: Sales, Marketing, and Seasonality
nodes.summary: The page describes the company’s end-to-end autonomous-driving solutions and customer access to its intellectual property through licensing and development agreements. Its global sales strategy relies on industry partners, technically skilled sales teams, application engineers, and solution architects; software-community engagement, early developer access, and AI training; and direct sales to cloud, enterprise, retail, and consumer customers. It also explains that revenue seasonality varies by market and product, was disrupted by excess supply in fiscal 2023, and may not follow historical patterns.

nodes.title: Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The company uses a fabless model, outsourcing wafer fabrication, assembly, testing, and packaging to certified suppliers to avoid manufacturing costs and risks and focus on design, quality assurance, marketing, and support. It may directly buy some materials, while suppliers procure most; it sometimes places advance non-cancellable orders, pays premiums, or deposits to secure components and capacity. Supplier relationships provide redundancy across wafer, assembly, testing, packaging, adapter card, switch, cable, substrate, and memory production. The company may consign key components, performs incoming quality checks and configuration, then ships semiconductors from third-party warehouses to contract manufacturers or customers, who assemble and test boards to its specifications and deliver products to retailers, system builders, or OEMs.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The market is intensely competitive, rapidly changing, and shaped by evolving standards. Success depends on performance, product breadth, customer and partner access, distribution, software and API support, manufacturing, pricing, and system costs, as well as anticipating demand and delivering quality products reliably at competitive prices. Competition is expected to grow, including from lower-priced or higher-performing products, new entrants, and alliances; some rivals have greater resources or adaptability. Competitors include GPU, CPU, DPU, SoC, and accelerated-computing suppliers; cloud companies developing in-house chips and software; Arm CPU and SoC providers; and interconnect, switching, cabling, and DPU suppliers, including AMD, Intel, major cloud providers, semiconductor firms, networking companies, and internal design teams.

nodes.title: Patents and Proprietary Rights
nodes.summary: The company protects its U.S. and international intellectual property through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, nondisclosure agreements, licenses, and foreign laws and treaties. Its issued patents expire from March 2023 to June 2045, with additional patents allowed or pending, mainly covering its products and related technology. Some countries, including in Asia, provide weaker protection, increasing piracy risks. The company evaluates where to seek formal protection based on manufacturing locations, regional strategies, enforceability of IP laws, and commercial significance, and it licenses and expects to continue licensing third-party technology.

nodes.title: Government Regulations
nodes.summary: The text outlines NVIDIA’s regulatory exposure, including new U.S. export-license requirements affecting some data-center products shipped to China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Russia; acquisition reviews and the terminated Arm deal, which resulted in a $1.35 billion write-off; and potential costs and business impacts from a broad range of current or future regulations. It describes ESG oversight, annual assessments, and reporting; climate-risk evaluation, renewable-energy goals, energy-efficient GPUs, Green500 results, and the planned Earth-2 climate digital twin. It also reports workforce size and roles, the need to recruit and retain talent, and global hiring efforts amid competition for technical talent.

nodes.title: ESG, Climate Change, and Human Capital
nodes.summary: NVIDIA integrates ESG principles across its business, with Board committee oversight and annual assessment; further information and related risks are identified. It assesses climate impacts and regulatory risks, reports environmental metrics, targets matching all office and data-center electricity use with renewable energy by fiscal 2025, and emphasizes energy-efficient products, including strong Green500 results. Its planned Earth-2 digital twin will support climate prediction and mitigation planning. At fiscal 2023 year-end, NVIDIA had 26,196 employees across 35 countries, and relies on recruiting, developing, and retaining talented staff to execute its strategy.

nodes.title: Recruitment
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its global technical recruiting, university and industry engagement, employee referrals, pandemic-related hiring flexibility, and fiscal 2023 hiring slowdown; its workforce is largely technical and highly educated. Development and retention efforts include training, coaching, learning programs, tuition support, internal mobility, targeted mentoring, employee-feedback channels, and a 5.3% turnover rate. Compensation includes performance-linked equity, while benefits support financial, physical, and mental well-being and are tailored to regional and community needs. The company promotes inclusion and diverse hiring, especially for historically underrepresented groups, through community partnerships and dedicated recruiting support.

nodes.title: Employee Development, Retention, Compensation, and Well-Being
nodes.summary: The page describes a flexible, largely technical workforce, FY2023 hiring slowdown, university and industry recruiting, and employee referrals. It covers development through training, coaching, learning resources, tuition support, internal mobility, and targeted mentoring; employee feedback channels and 5.3% turnover; performance-linked, time-vesting equity; and global benefits for physical, mental, and financial well-being, including retirement, stock purchase, flexibility, and tailored family and community support.

nodes.title: Diversity and Inclusion
nodes.summary: The text describes NVIDIA’s diversity and inclusion commitments, including efforts to recruit, develop, and retain historically underrepresented talent through partnerships, dedicated recruiting, leadership programs, resource groups, training, diverse candidate pools, and progress tracking. It reports fiscal 2023 workforce demographics: 80% male, 19% female, 1% undeclared globally, and 6% Black/African American or Hispanic/Latino employees in the U.S. It also covers health and safety support, hybrid work options and related well-being, remote-work, and social programs, plus company-wide rest days planned for fiscal 2024. Finally, it lists five executive officers, their ages and roles as of February 17, 2023, and provides career and education details for CEO Jen-Hsun Huang and CFO Colette M. Kress.

nodes.title: Workforce Diversity, Health, and Hybrid Work
nodes.summary: The text outlines diversity efforts: inclusion recruiting partners, women’s leadership development, support for nine employee resource groups, manager and peer training, diverse candidate pools, and progress tracking. At fiscal 2023 year-end, the workforce was 80% male, 19% female, and 1% undeclared; 6% of U.S. employees were Black or African American or Hispanic or Latino. The company prioritized employee and family health and safety during COVID-19, supported hybrid work with well-being programs, remote-work learning, and virtual social connection, and planned continued flexibility and company-wide rest days in fiscal 2024.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets
nodes.summary: NVIDIA identifies risks that could harm its business, financial condition, results, or reputation, lower its stock price, and cause investors to lose some or all of their investment. Unknown risks or those currently considered immaterial may also have adverse effects. Industry and market risks include failing to meet evolving needs and losing market share or revenue to competitors.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks involving demand forecasting, supplier dependence, manufacturing quality and product defects; global operations, economic and geopolitical conditions, cybersecurity, disruptions, climate change, acquisitions, customer concentration, talent, systems, COVID-19 and volatile results; and regulatory, ESG, responsible AI, intellectual property, privacy, tax, litigation, debt, and governance or contractual provisions that may affect control of the company.

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Rapid technological, customer, competitive, and standards changes threaten NVIDIA’s results if it cannot adapt products and strategies, invest in R&D, launch new business and service models, expand its ecosystem, meet safety and compliance requirements, manage product lifecycles, scale infrastructure and integrations, support customers, and fund necessary technical and commercial efforts. R&D in newer markets may take years to generate revenue or fail; adoption and customer value are uncertain, and lengthy design wins do not guarantee revenue, while losing one may hinder future wins. NVIDIA’s AI cloud and standalone software offerings—including DGX Cloud, pretrained models, AI Enterprise, Omniverse, and DRIVE—require substantial time and investment, may not succeed or generate meaningful revenue, despite multiyear cloud-hosting agreements.

nodes.title: Competition in our current and target markets could cause us to lose market share and revenue.
nodes.summary: Competition in current and target markets may intensify as offerings, standards, customer needs, entrants, and consolidations change. Competitors may offer cheaper or better products and have advantages in facilities, experience, customers, IP, designs, resources, market opportunities, product transitions, and supply access, potentially reducing prices and limiting market share. Customers may develop in-house substitutes, while competing cloud services could hinder the company’s AI offerings from achieving scale. Failure to compete could reduce demand and revenue.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply and Manufacturing Failure to estimate customer demand properly has led and could lead to mismatches between supply and demand.
nodes.summary: The company faces demand-forecasting and supply/manufacturing risks because it relies on third parties, lacks guaranteed capacity, and commits to inventory and supply in advance. Forecast errors, shortages, long lead times, excess or obsolete inventory, price changes, cancellation costs, and impaired commitments can disrupt sales, damage customer relationships and market share, and reduce margins and financial results. Demand volatility stems from competition, economic and health events, technology and product transitions, customer and channel behavior, AI/cloud services, gaming restrictions, cryptocurrency, and new or uncertain applications. Supply commitments and prepayments have grown, sometimes exceeding half of total supply, and may be difficult to reduce. Risks include transition execution and simultaneous product architectures, component constraints, disasters, pandemics, and Taiwan-China tensions. GPU mining, changing crypto markets and standards, resale and gray markets also complicate forecasts. Finally, demand depends on developers and content providers supporting the company’s platforms on acceptable terms.

nodes.title: Dependency on third-party suppliers and their technology to manufacture, assemble, test, package or design our products reduces our control over product quantity and quality, manufacturing yields, development, enhancement and product delivery schedules and could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company relies on third-party foundries, subcontractors, suppliers, and software tools to manufacture, assemble, test, package, and design its products, limiting control over quality, quantity, yields, development, and delivery. Risks include inaccurate demand forecasts and supply shortages or higher prices; inadequate materials or capacity; process-technology limitations and transitions; supplier concentration or loss; costs and delays in qualifying replacements; unqualified supplier changes; suppliers prioritizing others; inflexible or prepaid orders; low yields; and manufacturing disruptions from heat, natural disasters, or electricity conservation. These issues could constrain customer demand and supply-chain scaling and harm operations, margins, revenue, and financial results.

nodes.title: Defects in our products have caused and could cause us to incur significant expenses to remediate, which can damage our reputation and cause us to lose market share.
nodes.summary: Product defects, failures, or security vulnerabilities may trigger costly repairs, recalls, write-offs, customer reimbursements, regulatory fines, litigation, and loss of reputation, market share, design wins, and revenue; partner-supplied components reduce production control, and remedies or insurance may be inadequate. A third-party component defect in Data Center products caused a fiscal 2023 warranty liability, which may require adjustment. Economic downturns, inflation, policy shifts, higher costs and interest rates, weak demand, supply disruptions, insolvencies, and financial-market risks could harm operations and results. Worldwide operations and offshore manufacturing expose the company to economic, political, legal, cultural, health, currency, and catastrophic-event risks; 69% of fiscal 2023 revenue came from outside the U.S.

nodes.title: Global Business Risks and Economic Uncertainty
key_items: Risks Related to Our Global Operating Business Adverse economic conditions may harm our business.
International operations are a significant part of our business, which exposes us to us to risks that could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The page describes product-defect and liability risks, including warranty costs, claims, and potentially inadequate insurance. It explains how adverse economic conditions can raise costs, reduce demand and margins, disrupt supply, constrain forecasting and financing, and cause counterparty failures. It also outlines risks from extensive international operations, including overseas manufacturing and sales, differing political, legal, and business conditions, health-related lockdowns, currency and capital-market disruptions, and disasters or conflict.

nodes.title: Product, system security, and data protection breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue and increase our expenses, which could adversely affect our stock price and damage our reputation.
nodes.summary: The text warns that increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks—including ransomware, geopolitical attacks, and supply-chain breaches—could disrupt operations, compromise company, partner, and customer data, expose proprietary game source code, and cause liability, regulatory action, reputational damage, lost sales, higher costs, and stock-price harm. Defenses, vulnerability remediation, and supplier oversight require ongoing investment but cannot eliminate risk. It also describes business-disruption risks from disasters, extreme weather, utility and cloud outages, violence, war, pandemics, political instability, and geopolitical tensions, especially given operational and supplier concentration in California and Asia and activities in Israel. Such events could disrupt manufacturing, logistics, markets, staffing, and operations, raising expenses and harming revenue and results.

nodes.title: Climate change may have a long-term impact on our business.
nodes.summary: Climate change may disrupt the company, its customers, suppliers, and partners through resource constraints, extreme weather, wildfire-related power shutoffs, supply-chain and infrastructure damage, and political instability, causing operational interruptions, attrition, losses, and higher costs. Insurance may not cover losses adequately. Climate-related laws, regulations, and lawsuits could increase direct and indirect costs, require operational or product-design changes, and create litigation or reputational risks. The company may miss its 2025 renewable-electricity goal or incur unexpected costs, and climate disruptions may cause contractual disputes. Climate concerns may also reduce demand for energy-intensive products or raise efficiency expectations.

nodes.title: We may not be able to realize the potential benefits of business investments or acquisitions, and we may not be able to successfully integrate acquisition targets, which could hurt our ability to grow our business, develop new products or sell our products.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from acquisitions and strategic investments, including failed or delayed deals, regulatory barriers, integration difficulties, financial costs, liabilities, cybersecurity exposure, and failure to realize benefits; it cites the terminated NVIDIA–Arm deal and a $1.35 billion write-off. It also warns that integration problems have disrupted operations. Revenue depends on a limited set of partners and customers whose purchases, sales, or ability to buy may change. Talent shortages, retention, compensation, immigration, and succession risks could harm execution. Finally, ERP and other business-system disruptions or control implementation failures could impair operations and financial reporting.

nodes.title: Acquisition, Customer, and Workforce Risks
key_items: We receive a significant amount of our revenue from a limited number of customers and our revenue could be adversely affected if we lose or are prevented from selling to any of these customers.
If we are unable to attract, retain and motivate our executives and key employees, our business may be harmed.
nodes.summary: The text describes acquisition risks, including adverse economic changes, cybersecurity exposure, inadequate due diligence, relationship or personnel losses, and costly, disruptive systems integration that can hurt results. It also warns that revenue depends on a limited number of distribution and partner customers whose purchasing patterns, sales, or ability to buy may change, and that customer losses, trade restrictions, or collection problems could harm financial results. Finally, it notes challenges in attracting, retaining, and motivating diverse talent amid labor competition, inflation, pandemic and immigration factors, rising compensation costs, reduced stock-compensation retention, and the need for executive succession and smooth transitions.

nodes.title: Our business is dependent upon the proper functioning of our business processes and information systems and modification or interruption of such systems may disrupt our business, processes and internal controls.
nodes.summary: The text warns that reliance on business processes and information systems, including ongoing ERP implementation, creates risks of operational disruption, reporting errors, costly implementation, and failures in controls or reporting obligations. Material weaknesses could undermine investor confidence, require costly remediation or restatements, restrict capital-market access, lower share value, and trigger regulatory action. COVID-19 may disrupt employees, operations, customers, suppliers, supply chains, China sales, and financial markets; response measures add costs, and impacts remain difficult to predict and may compound other risks. Results may fluctuate, and missed expectations could reduce the stock price. Drivers include limited spending flexibility, contractual compliance, customer payment and credit risks, vendor payment demands, environmental costs, and accounting changes; extended customer terms and shorter vendor terms can constrain cash flow.

nodes.title: Financial Reporting, COVID-19, and Operating Risks
key_items: The COVID-19 pandemic has affected and could continue to have a material adverse impact on our financial condition and results of operations.

Our operating results have in the past fluctuated and may in the future fluctuate, and if our operating results are below the expectations of securities analysts or investors, our stock price could decline.
nodes.summary: The page warns that internal-control material weaknesses may undermine confidence, require costly remediation or restatements, delay reporting, restrict capital-market access, and trigger regulatory action. COVID-19 may disrupt operations, employees, customers, suppliers, supply chains, China sales, and financial markets; responses may add costs, and impacts are hard to predict and may compound other risks. Results may fluctuate due to spending constraints, contractual and payment issues, vendor terms, environmental costs, and accounting changes. Missed expectations or reduced cash flow could cause stock-price declines or volatility.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock and Other Matters Our operations could be affected by the complex laws, rules and regulations to which our business is subject, and political and other actions may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from complex and changing global laws and regulations, including compliance costs, penalties, reputational harm, operational restrictions, and political actions. Trade controls, sanctions, tariffs, and export licensing can disrupt shipments, services, supply chains, and sales; the Ukraine war halted business in Russia and affected EMEA demand. Growing AI-related export controls may constrain products, markets, manufacturing, and R&D, create competitive disadvantages, and reduce revenue. U.S. restrictions targeting China affect NVIDIA chips and systems, require operational transitions, and may cause licensing delays, customer losses, excess inventory, and costs. Chinese gaming and digital-platform restrictions may also reduce Gaming and Data Center revenue.

nodes.title: Increased scrutiny from shareholders, regulators and others regarding our environmental, social and governance responsibilities could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from rising ESG and sustainability scrutiny, including compliance costs, unmet stakeholder expectations, reputational damage, lost business, and liability. Responsible AI use may create ethical, regulatory, financial, competitive, adoption, and reputational risks. IP disputes and protection efforts can incur costs, damages, injunctions, licensing obligations, business interruption, and loss of competitive advantage, while foreign-law limits, theft, employee departures, and uncertain protection approvals threaten IP. The text also introduces risks from changing privacy and security obligations governing sensitive, confidential, and personal data.

nodes.title: AI Responsibility and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: Issues relating to the responsible use of our technologies, including AI in our offerings, may result in reputational and financial harm and liability.

Actions to adequately protect our IP rights could result in substantial costs to us and our ability to compete could be harmed if we are unsuccessful or if we are prohibited from making or selling our products.
nodes.summary: The text warns that customer concerns or business decisions related to company policies may harm its reputation and business or create liability. Responsible use of AI and other evolving technologies presents ethical, regulatory, reputational, competitive, legal, and financial risks that could raise costs or slow adoption. IP disputes may bring legal expenses, damages, injunctions, licensing costs, or product suspensions; pursuing enforcement can also be costly and trigger countersuits. Protection depends on legal and contractual measures that may be weaker abroad, while theft, employee moves, and uncertain protection applications could undermine competitive advantage and returns on investment.

nodes.title: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws, rules, regulations, and other obligations. Privacy or security concerns relating to our products and services could damage our reputation, deter current and potential customers, or result in legal or regulatory proceedings and liability.
nodes.summary: The text warns that evolving privacy and security laws, contractual duties, policies, and public statements expose the company to reputational harm, customer loss, costs, business disruption, litigation, and regulatory penalties if data is misused, breached, or handled improperly, including in AI-related uses. It outlines U.S. state and federal rules, California’s CCPA/CPRA, other state laws, GDPR and U.K. GDPR, and proposed EU AI regulation. Cross-border transfer and localization rules, especially in Europe and China, may restrict data movement and raise costs. Compliance obligations may require operational changes; failures can trigger enforcement, fines, lawsuits, oversight, processing bans, or data destruction.

nodes.title: We have exposure to additional tax liabilities and our operating results may be adversely impacted by higher than expected tax rates and other tax-related factors.
nodes.summary: Complex global income and non-income tax rules, judgment in tax estimates, and ongoing audits—including U.S. fiscal 2018–2019 and audits in Germany, Israel, and India—could lead to additional liabilities and harm financial results and cash flows. U.S. tax changes, including the Inflation Reduction Act, potential higher rates or reduced FDII benefits, and OECD-driven foreign tax reforms may raise taxes or uncertainty. Future effective tax rates may also vary with business and earnings mix, rates, incentives, deductions, audit outcomes, accounting and tax-return adjustments, nondeductible expenses, deferred-tax valuations, legal interpretations, acquisitions, organizational changes, and stock-based compensation and share-price fluctuations.

nodes.title: Our business is exposed to the risks associated with litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings.
nodes.summary: The company faces ongoing litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings that may be costly, disruptive, and result in damages, fines, injunctions, or other material effects; it is appealing dismissal of a securities class action concerning statements about channel inventory and cryptocurrency-mining GPU demand. Its $11 billion of notes due through 2060 and $575 million commercial paper program create repayment, refinancing, cash-flow, covenant, financing, and strategic risks, including possible acceleration after covenant breaches and effects from credit-rating changes. Delaware law, corporate governance provisions, and Microsoft’s Xbox-related stock purchase rights may impede takeovers and shareholder actions. Staff comments are not applicable. Properties include headquarters and other owned or leased offices, data centers, R&D, sales, and administrative facilities in the U.S. and abroad; facilities are considered suitable, and lease details are incorporated by reference.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Business Overview, Challenges, and AI Services
key_items: Recent Developments, Future Objectives and Challenges Supply, Products Transitions, and New Products and Business Models
nodes.summary: The page introduces NVIDIA’s management discussion and advises readers to consider its risk factors and financial statements. Operating expenses increased 50%, including a $1.35 billion Arm deal termination charge and higher compensation, infrastructure, and engineering costs. summary: Canadian RSUs must be settled only in shares, not cash. Quebec residents receive French translations of the Plan and Agreement, which govern unless they choose otherwise. A data-privacy supplement authorizes information gathering, sharing with advisors, and storage in employee files. Shares may be resold through the company’s designated broker only outside Canada via a stock exchange. Canadian residents may need to report specified foreign property on Form T1135 when its cost exceeds C$100,000; RSUs are generally reported at nil cost, and share cost is generally fair market value at acquisition, potentially averaged with other shares. Consult a tax advisor.

title: CHINA
summary: China: Awards vest only while required SAFE approvals remain valid; shares may be sold at vesting or later through the designated broker, with net proceeds paid subject to taxes and exchange rules. If sale is not required at vesting, shares must be sold within 90 days after service ends or may be sold compulsorily. Proceeds and dividends must be repatriated through a company-established Chinese exchange-control account; payment may be in U.S. dollars or local currency, with currency risk borne by the participant. Shares must remain in the Plan account and cannot otherwise be transferred or pledged. Participants must meet future Company exchange-control requirements. Czech Republic: Participants may have CNB reporting duties for shares, dividends, and foreign accounts and should seek advice; compliance is their responsibility. Denmark: Employees acknowledge receipt of the Danish-language Employer Statement; for awards from January 1, 2019, Agreement and Plan termination provisions apply under the amended Stock Option Act. Foreign accounts holding shares or cash must be reported to the Danish Tax Administration.

title: China, Czech Republic, and Denmark Equity Plan Terms
summary: The text requires China-based award proceeds or dividends to pass through a special account, permits payment in U.S. dollars or local currency, explains related account and exchange-rate responsibilities, and requires compliance with future exchange-control rules. Czech participants may have CNB notification duties for shares, dividends, and foreign accounts and must check current rules. Danish participants acknowledge receipt of the Danish-language Employer Statement and the post-2019 termination provisions under the Stock Option Act; foreign share or cash accounts must be reported to the Danish Tax Administration.

title: SPECIAL NOTICE FOR EMPLOYEES IN DENMARK SÆRLIG MEDDELELSE TIL MEDARBEJDERE I
summary: Bilingual Danish-English employer statement under Denmark’s Stock Option Act explains NVIDIA RSU grants under its 2007 Equity Incentive Plan, noting further terms are in the Plan and Agreement. It covers grant date, the Board’s discretion over future grants and Plan changes, vesting subject to continuous service and conversion to shares, no purchase or exercise payment, forfeiture of unvested RSUs upon termination (except death), and financial effects: no immediate consequences or inclusion in salary-based benefits, while shares carry market risk and uncertain value.

title: Finland and France Award Provisions
summary: Finland has no country-specific provisions. In France, the restricted stock units are not intended to receive specified French tax and social-security treatment. Award acceptance confirms that the recipient read and understood the Plan and Agreement, provided in English; this consent is stated in both English and French. French residents must report foreign cash, securities, and bank or brokerage accounts, including accounts opened or closed during the tax year, on their annual tax return; failure may result in significant penalties.

title: GERMANY
summary: Germany requires Bundesbank reporting of qualifying securities transactions, acquisitions, sales, and dividends exceeding €12,500, generally monthly through its portal or another permitted method. Residents must report certain large or substantial shareholdings to their local tax office, subject to an exception for qualifying U.S.-listed shares when ownership is below 1%. Greece and Hungary have no country-specific provisions. In Hong Kong, RSUs must settle in shares; shares issued within six months may not be publicly offered or disposed of during that period. The award is a private, unreviewed offer for eligible service providers, with a warning to seek independent advice. India requires repatriation and conversion of sale proceeds and dividends within applicable deadlines.

title: Greece, Hong Kong, and Hungary Award Provisions
summary: Greece and Hungary have no country-specific provisions. For Hong Kong, restricted stock units must be settled in shares, not cash; shares are a personal investment, and shares issued within six months of grant may not be publicly offered or disposed of during that period. A securities notice warns that the materials are unreviewed by Hong Kong regulators, advises independent professional advice, states the award is not a public offering or prospectus, and restricts materials to eligible service providers’ personal use.

title: INDIA
summary: Indian participants must repatriate proceeds from share sales and dividends to India, convert them to local currency within legally prescribed timelines, obtain and retain a bank-issued FIRC as proof, and comply with exchange-control rules, seeking legal advice as needed. Indian residents must report foreign assets, including plan shares, and foreign bank accounts over which they have signing authority in annual tax returns, and should consult a tax advisor to ensure compliance.

title: INDONESIA
summary: Indonesian participants accepting the award confirm they read and understand the English Plan and Agreement, accept their terms, and agree not to challenge the document’s validity under Indonesia’s language law or implementing regulation. Indonesian residents must report worldwide assets, including foreign accounts and plan shares, on annual tax returns and report foreign-exchange remittances to Bank Indonesia monthly online. Banks handling remittances of share-sale proceeds or dividends into Indonesia also report transactions for statistical purposes and may request supporting information and documents from the participant.

title: ISRAEL
summary: For participants in Israel on the grant date, awards are governed by the Israeli sub-plan, Section 102 capital-gains rules, applicable tax rulings and the Trust Agreement. Awards are held by a company-appointed trustee, subject to a lockup and release only after the required period and full tax payment; participants must meet trustee requirements, and the company or trustee may withhold taxes. Trustee-102 status depends on Israeli Tax Authority approval; absent approval, awards are non-trustee awards unless the Authority decides otherwise. The company does not guarantee tax qualification or owe damages if it is lost. For participants who transfer to Israel after grant, the company may require immediate sale of vested shares, with proceeds paid net of taxes and broker charges.

title: ITALY
summary: Italian participants acknowledge receiving, reviewing, understanding, and accepting the Plan and Agreement, and expressly approving specified provisions on legal compliance, transfer limits, taxes, grant nature, additional requirements, governing law and venue, and EU/EEA/Swiss/UK data privacy. Italian residents may have annual tax-return reporting duties for foreign investments or financial assets that may generate taxable income, including when beneficial owners under anti-money-laundering rules. Shares and certain other foreign assets held abroad may also be subject to tax based on their year-end fair market value; participants should consult personal tax advisers.

title: Japan and Korea Reporting Notifications
summary: Japan: Residents must report foreign assets exceeding ¥50 million in net fair market value as of December 31 by March 15, and report single stock acquisitions valued above ¥100 million to the Ministry of Finance through the Bank of Japan within 20 days; tax advice is recommended. Korea: Residents must declare foreign accounts and file a report if their month-end balance exceeds KRW 500 million (or equivalent) in any month of the calendar year.

title: MALAYSIA
summary: Malaysia-specific terms replace the prior data-privacy consent: participants voluntarily authorize the Company, service recipient, affiliates, Schwab, and other providers to collect, use, retain, and transfer personal and equity-plan data to administer the plan, including across borders with potentially different privacy protections. Participants may request recipient details, access or correct data, learn about its processing, or refuse or withdraw consent in writing without cost; employment and career are unaffected, but future awards or plan administration may be unavailable. Questions about consequences may be sent to NVIDIA-StockAdmin@nvidia.com. Directors of Malaysian affiliates must notify the affiliate in writing within 14 days of acquiring or disposing of an interest in the Company or an affiliate.

title: MEXICO
key_items: (1) Su participación en el Plan no constituye un derecho adquirido;
(2) El Plan y su participación en el Plan se ofrecen por la Compañía de una manera totalmente discrecional;
summary: The Mexico terms state that accepting the award confirms receipt and acceptance of the Plan and Agreement and approval of Section 11: participation is voluntary, discretionary, creates no acquired rights or compensation claims, and the Company and affiliates are not liable for share-value decreases. The Company administers the Plan, but it creates no employment or service relationship or benefits with NVIDIA Mexico and does not affect continuous-service terms; the Company may change or end participation, and the participant releases related claims. A Spanish translation repeats these acknowledgements. Securities notices explain that awards and shares are unregistered and cannot be publicly offered or distributed in Mexico; materials are private, for current Company or affiliate employees and contractors, may not be copied, and associated rights are non-transferable.

title: Country-Specific Plan Notices
summary: Norway has no country-specific provisions. Palestine residents may have tax, exchange-control, or foreign-asset reporting obligations related to plan shares or proceeds and should consult a legal adviser. In Poland, transfers above €15,000 (or PLN 15,000 for business activity) must use a Polish bank account; transaction records must be kept for five years, and residents with foreign securities or accounts exceeding PLN 7 million in combined overseas assets may need quarterly National Bank reports. Saudi Arabia restricts document distribution to permitted persons, disclaims responsibility for its accuracy, and advises prospective purchasers to conduct due diligence and consult an authorized financial adviser if needed.

title: SINGAPORE
summary: Singapore terms prohibit sale of shares acquired through Restricted Stock Units for six months after grant, except under specified SFA exemptions or other applicable SFA provisions. The award relies on the SFA Qualifying Person exemption, is exempt from prospectus and registration requirements, is not intended for onward sale, and the Plan is not registered as a prospectus. Singapore Affiliate directors must report specified interest acquisitions, disposals, changes, or relevant appointments in writing within two business days, regardless of residence or employment; these rules may also apply to a Singapore Affiliate CEO.

title: SOUTH AFRICA
summary: For South African employees, the terms supplement Section 10 of the Global RSU Agreement: employees must promptly report income realized at vesting and settlement to the Service Recipient or risk a fine, and are responsible for any tax shortfall beyond amounts withheld. Award holders must also ensure compliance with South African exchange control laws and are advised to consult a personal legal adviser.

title: SPAIN
summary: Spanish terms state that accepting the award confirms Plan participation and receipt of the Plan; the discretionary, gratuitous award is not employment compensation, a guaranteed benefit, or part of a service contract. Participation requires active continued service and generally ends immediately upon termination for any reason except death, including dismissal or changes or breaches of service terms. The award is not a Spanish public securities offering or registered prospectus. Reporting rules cover D-6 declarations for certain substantial holdings and transactions, Form 720 reporting of foreign assets over €50,000 (with later reporting if value rises over €20,000), and Bank of Spain reporting of foreign securities accounts above €1 million; residents should seek personal tax and legal advice.

title: SWEDEN
summary: Sweden authorizes the company or service recipient to withhold or sell shares at vesting or settlement to cover tax-related items, even when not required to withhold. Switzerland’s private award offering is unregistered, is not a FinSA prospectus, may not be publicly distributed, and has not been submitted to or approved or supervised by Swiss authorities. Taiwan limits Plan participation to company and affiliate personnel, states the offer is not public, and sets foreign-currency remittance limits and documentation requirements, with legal advice recommended. Thai residents must repatriate proceeds of at least US$1 million per transaction, convert or deposit them within 360 days, and report the remittance to the Bank of Thailand.

title: Switzerland and Taiwan Award Notices
summary: Switzerland: The Award is a private offering, not subject to registration, and the related materials are not a FinSA prospectus, cannot be publicly distributed beyond Company or Service Recipient employees, and have not been or will be reviewed or approved by Swiss authorities. Taiwan: Plan participation is limited to Consultants, Directors, and Employees of the Company and its Affiliates and is not a public securities offer by a Taiwanese company. Residents may remit foreign currency up to US$5 million annually without justification; transactions of TWD 500,000 or more require a form and supporting documents, while transactions of US$500,000 or more may require additional documents. Residents should seek legal advice on compliance.

title: THAILAND
summary: Thailand: Residents receiving US$1 million or more from a single share sale or dividend must promptly repatriate funds, then convert them to baht or deposit them in a Thai foreign-currency account within 360 days; inward remittances of that size must be reported to the Bank of Thailand. Noncompliance may incur penalties; regulations change, so seek legal advice, and individuals are responsible for compliance. Türkiye: Plan shares cannot be sold within Türkiye but may be sold on Nasdaq; foreign-securities investment activity must go through a licensed bank or intermediary and be reported to the Capital Markets Board, with the participant responsible for compliance. Ukraine: Participants must comply with exchange controls and should consult a lawyer before opening foreign accounts or acquiring or selling shares. UAE (Dubai): The Plan is offered only to eligible service providers and may not be distributed to or relied on by others. Purchasers should conduct due diligence and seek authorized financial advice if needed; relevant UAE authorities have not reviewed, verified, or approved the Plan or Agreement and disclaim responsibility.

title: Türkiye, Ukraine, and Dubai Plan Notices
summary: The page notes that Thai exchange-control violations may incur Bank of Thailand penalties, regulations can change without notice, and individuals are responsible for compliance and related fines. Türkiye residents may sell plan shares through Nasdaq, not within Türkiye, and foreign-securities transactions must use a licensed intermediary and be reported to the Capital Markets Board. Ukraine participants are responsible for exchange-control compliance and are advised to seek legal advice before opening foreign accounts or trading shares. In Dubai, the plan is limited to eligible service providers; recipients should conduct due diligence and consult an authorized adviser if needed. Relevant UAE authorities have not reviewed, verified, or approved the plan documents.

title: UNITED KINGDOM
summary: For UK residents, restricted stock units must be settled only in common shares, never cash. Participants are responsible for all tax-related items and must pay them when requested and indemnify the company and service recipient for amounts they pay or withhold. Directors and executive officers may be unable to indemnify unpaid income tax if that would constitute a loan. Tax unpaid within 90 days after the relevant UK tax year may become a taxable benefit, requiring the participant to report and pay income tax to HMRC and reimburse related National Insurance contributions.
